title: Following Politics: Russian Youth Activism in Post-Socialist Latvia
abstract: My dissertation is based on fieldwork conducted in Latvia. Latvia is frequently introduced with a demographic statistic which characterizes 60% of its population as Latvian and 40% as Russian. The ensuing discussion focuses on nationalism and ethnic tensions--terms central to scholarship on Eastern Europe. Below, I problematize the ubiquity of these terms in accounts of post-socialist politics. Drawing on ethnographic research with Latvia's Russian youth organizations, I argue that these terms obscure a phenomenon that has an important empirical bearing: the fact that actors, who are by no means marginal in electoral politics, have a stake in remaining legible within a sphere of action characterized by ethnic division; and, at the same time, challenge forms of action based on ethnic solidarity.Recent events in Ukraine have once again brought to the fore the problematic role of ethnic Russians in post-Soviet republics. In much of political commentary Russians living outside of the Russian Federation appear as pawns of Kremlin's attempt to regain its dominance over the post-soviet world; as subjects injured by nationalizing elites' attempt to undo effects of Soviet Russification; and, fundamentally, as reactionary supporters of a (pro-) Russian autocracy. In fact, over the last decade policy makers from the European Union have spent a great deal of effort working with Russian activists in Eastern Europe in a hope to shift their political allegiances; to teach them the value of national sovereignty; and, fundamentally, to get them to differentiate between democratic freedoms (inherent in European institutions) and selective privileges (held over from the Soviet period). In my dissertation, I challenge the assumption that Russians living outside the Russian Federation are pawns of Muscovite expansion, and, in the same vein, critique the hope that they make become agents of European democratization. Analyzing Latvia's Russian youth activists' ambitious for meaningful elected office, I argue that despite having different geopolitical and ideological orientations, EU- and RF-programs are equally likely to perpetuate parliamentary gridlock, voter apathy, and anti-political sentiment. In a related vein, I explore how youth activists turn to late-socialist practices in an attempt to create viable alternatives to both "pro-Russian" and "pro-European" positions; and how these alternatives have immense potential to draw together young people of different ideological persuasions, ethnic identities and life styles.

title: Silent Witness
abstract: New research suggests that butterflies and moths come with mental baggage…left over from their lives as larvae.—ScienceHe’d like to be at one with his new selfbut memories sit in him like eyes.Sometimes scent implies an unheard-ofidea and he’s offbut it’s just another of the given forms.You’d think flight would be decent redress,the power to sift himself through airand leave each thought in its old place,where hard feelings also could be left.He shrugs and the wingsquiver with great precision,nature will have to live with what it’s done,he cannot manage even resignationwithout a show of grace.—Jana Prikryl, “The Moth” (2015)Recently I woke up to a provocative little news story. A popular software coding company called Cursor was thrown into crisis by a wayward AI system deployed to handle its customer service. Apparently a chatbot, posturing as a human named “Sam,” invented an explanation for a glitch that was logging users out when they switched between devices. With no human oversight, “Sam” told callers that logouts were “expected behavior” given “a new login policy”; in fact, there was no such policy. Rather, the AI generator was “hallucinating”—as AI technology is wont to do. The company lost a great deal of business when frustrated customers just gave up. As an AI tech advisor later posted: “This mess could have been avoided if leaders understood that (1) AI makes mistakes, (2) AI can’t take responsibility for those mistakes (so it falls on you), and (3) users hate being tricked by a machine posing as a human.”1 It honestly reminded me of the parenting advice one might give to someone who’d left their toddler at home alone to play with the stove.A techie friend describes his relation to artificial intelligence as “productive dreaming.” I suppose I shouldn’t have been surprised: the ineffably messy language models upon which AI feeds seem very much like Jungian dreams. Assemblages are made, images composed, patterns matched, meaning extracted—even when the guiding logic is not always made clear. Still, I had never thought to pair dreams and productivity. I came of age against a backdrop of Martin Luther King’s resonantly hopeful declaration that he had a dream. It was visionary, but not in a way that implied economic “productivity” or specific material outcome. So perhaps that is why my dreams come to me as lush visitations, relaxed wool-gathering, a freely wandering substance-without-substance, untethered to notions of “product.”In contrast, my friend seemed to think of AI as merely a technocratically expedited way of dreaming, a way to rapidly harness a universe of information, attach a search function, then simply press the Button of Instrumentalization that will squeeze it all for monetized juice. He even advised that I gather up my “useless” dreams, “feed them to AI, and tell it to write you some movie scripts. You could be rich.”His advice jolted me. My pleasantly relaxed internal dream-generator came face to face with the transactional seductions of generative AI-ness. It left me wondering about the econometric design logic of our increasingly technologically mediated lives.I grew up dreaming of personhood as key to the recognition of my humanity. During the height of the civil rights movement of the 1960s, I knew only that I did not want to be a “second-class citizen.” Even as a child I knew that the status called “personhood”—the legal recognition of capacity as an autonomous individual—was a portal to the protections and grace of full civic belonging. I memorized the Fourteenth Amendment. I took to heart all the narrative strategies, rooted in language, that allowed a body to be seen. The politics of the day left no question as to what was at stake: rights of association and of public accommodation, land claims, intimacies of belonging, desegregating institutions, population-wide public health, refuting eugenic concepts. If there was no easy remedy for social divisions, one almost always had a pretty clear sense of what processes to follow in pursuing what we hoped would be justice. We reached for rules of evidence in law, we aimed for reproducible results in science, we pressed doctors to do no harm in the practice of medicine. We aspired to hearings and due process before depriving anyone of life or liberty.Unfortunately, contemporary metrics for social order have shifted in this neoliberal moment, and citizenship itself has shifted from being conceived as a “bundle of rights” to a model premised on human capitalization, pecuniary status, and asset acquisition (as in “golden passports.”)2 The old landmarks of civil rights address—those clear-edged solids, those visible goals—seem not only much less accessible but much less discernible in a world dedicated to the purity of productivity. The promise of personhood—as a commitment to notions of autonomy; rights to privacy, public accommodation, and franchise; equality; and civic belonging—seems to be dissolving. We are rapidly sinking into a disordered digital echo chamber.The story of “Sam,” the hallucinating chatbot, also captured my attention because so many of us work in offices that are cutting labor costs by introducing AI assistants. We may be instructed not just to learn to operate them but to “play” with them, “talk with them,” and “make friends” with our new robotic helpmeets. Moreover, learning to use these tools involves engaging with their various “emotions” and “personalities” and not just their mechanics. This phenomenon was underscored in a much-shared episode of the Ezra Klein show, during which his guest cited a study showing that “if you emotionally manipulate the A.I., you get better math results. So telling it your job depends on it gets you better results. Tipping, especially $20 or $100—saying, I’m about to tip you if you do well, seems to work pretty well. It performs slightly worse in December than May, and we think it’s because it has internalized the idea of winter break.”3I told my tech friend that this sort of AI hallucination strikes me as a phenomenon not too far removed from the carefree indulgences of my own disobedient dreams. I have an internal version of “Sam”—it just doesn’t get to rule the world. That dreamy fugue self is always exploring, inventing, collaging bits and bobs, and making stuff up, free-associating with legions of imaginary friends. Indeed, in the very early moments of generative AI, I loved the possibility of such unbounded humanoid whimsy softening the machine with an open-minded, interactive deus ex machina. But these days, I am increasingly apprehensive about what happens when AI begins to fill human dreams with the humanoid—when it ghost-visits me at that precise hinge in my half-conscious perception, the silky joint where the pleasant fog of sleep meets the hard edges of practical existence. What happens, in other words, when AI-ness disguises itself as a mirror of my desire and slides through a portal of “productively” nudged awakenings, posturing as sensed human experience.We all know that office computers are suddenly and ubiquitously preloaded with AI software that, at the most basic level, suggests punctuation, spelling, words, paragraphs, and a range of what might be logical choice points. It feels as fanciful and seamless as a dream, but it operates as a programmatic norming of language, too; it is only as creative as its database, and its database is really an emotionless remix—the lowest common denominator of a deceptively universalizing but very narrow slice of human experience (Western, Anglophile, quantitative, skewing to masculine modifiers). Its effectiveness as an autonomous support system for human beings “requires a level of empathy, nuance, and problem-solving that AI alone currently struggles to deliver,” explains Sanketh Balakrishna, an engineering manager at cloud security platform Datadog. “I would be cautious about depending entirely on an AI bot for addressing user issues.”4 ***Sherry Turkle is a social psychologist and founding director of MIT’s Initiative on Technology and Self. She has observed that in the early days of home computing, people couldn’t quite imagine how to “keep computers busy.” Dates and addresses were so easily and cheaply contained by paper calendars and rolodexes. It wasn’t that long ago, but there has been a seismic revolution: “Once we networked with each other, once computers were our portal to being with each other, we really don't have to worry about keeping computers busy. They keep us busy.” Indeed, we are not just tethered but addicted, sutured, chained to our screens, whether we want to be or not. It is practically impossible to function in the present industrialized world without the assistance of our handheld devices; busy indeed, they affirm our creditability, attest to our humanity. “These technologies are our current partners in the human adventure,” says Turkle. We must ask: “does it serve our human purposes?—a question that causes us to reconsider what these purposes are.”5In law, “the human adventure” is less defined by our biological “nature” than by juridical determinations of “personhood.” Law crafts personhood. Personhood confers agency, autonomy, equality, franchise, standing to sue, due process, and the capacity to access the privileges and immunities guaranteed by the Constitution. Personhood also refers to the rhetorical framings that infuse our various philosophical and religious conceptions of living subjects, legally anthropomorphized nonpersons, and culturally enchanted objects. Negotiating the relations and borders between human and subhuman, thinker and thing, autonomous being and automaton, is urgently consequential in an era of algorithmic assortment and mass surveillance.For some years, I have taught a class entitled “The Anatomy of Autonomy.” In it we study notions of individualism, configurations of citizenship, the civic vivacity of righted beings, the civil death of statelessness and incarceration, concepts of human capital, and legal fictions like corporate personhood. We read Aristotle, René Descartes, Ralph Waldo Emerson, tracking the underpinnings of notions like integrity of the body, the limits of one’s “private person,” and the hagiography of the singular agentic individual. We interrogate the features of an imagined ideal body, like Leonardo da Vinci’s Vitruvian Man, and how those metrics might undergird figurations of homo economicus, or the legal subject, or a rights-bearing citizen. We discuss how social value is sometimes tethered to temporal orderings—that is, concepts like nostalgic pasts or utopic futures—and how those orderings allow us to imagine ourselves as upwardly mobile, self-made, self-owning, self-regulating, free-willed choice-makers.For the last decade and a half, the single most exciting part of such a course was discussion of Citizens United v. title: Beyond Task Completion: Training Capable and Safe Computer-Use Agents
abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) have made rapid progress in completing complex tasks through graphical user interfaces, yet post-training centered on task success alone does not induce reliable safety behavior. A reliable CUA must condition its execution on risk: it should complete ordinary benign tasks, avoid environmental hazards and continue when a safe completion path remains, and refuse when the goal is harmful or no safe path exists. To learn this conditional policy, we develop Safety and Capability Optimization for Policy Execution (SCOPE), which jointly post-trains a CUA for task-execution capability and safety-aware decision making. To provide aligned training data for this joint objective, we further introduce SCOPE-Gen, an automated pipeline that synthesizes verifiable capability tasks and converts them into paired environment-risk variants while preserving their original goals. Using the resulting tasks, we construct SATraj-OS, a trajectory dataset comprising capability demonstrations, safe continuations, and explicit refusals. SCOPE first learns from all three trajectory types through supervised fine-tuning and then further improves task completion through online reinforcement learning. Starting from Qwen3.5-9B, SCOPE-RL achieves a 54.17% task success rate on OSWorld and a 64.30% attack-avoidance rate on OS-BLIND, yielding the best aggregate capability--safety score of 58.80% among the evaluated agents. Ablations reveal asymmetric but complementary roles for the two forms of safety supervision: refusal trajectories account for most of the attack-avoidance gain, whereas risk-handling trajectories preserve greater task utility at comparable attack-avoidance levels.

title: Politics, power and control in the British National Health Service - will anything really change?
abstract: The British National Health Service (NHS) was always going to be difficult to control and repeated structural reorganizations have been introduced throughout its history in the attempt to get the operational end of the service to do what Governments require of it. This has been easier said than done. A service that is free at the point of delivery and remains almost entirely supported by public funds is a constant political liability. The demand for health services is infinite but there is only a finite resource to pay for them. Consequently, Governments of any particular persuasion are vulnerable to the accusation that the service is being rationed and starved of essential resources. At the heart of all reorganizations, therefore, is the intention to contain costs by improving efficiency. The current reorganization, which is the most radical of any ever attempted, is no exception (DOH 2001). Changes have been proposed within the overall top level bureaucracy. But at the clinical level, where one finds service users, Primary Care Trusts (PCTs) will become the lead organization in assessing need and planning, purchasing and improving health services and the health status of the population. Secondary care will be provided under delivery agreements with PCTs by NHS Trusts. Within these organizations, it is intended to devolve greater responsibility to clinical teams than has been previously done. The constant claim of the current Government is that frontline staff will control frontline services and appropriate resources will be devolved to them to allow them to get on with the job of caring for patients (Milburn 2001). The alleged devolution of power suggests a loosening of Central Government interference, that has characterized the performance of the Labour Government since 1997. The record so far suggests that there is a strong central direction through a dogmatic political line from the Secretary of State for Health, through Regional Chairs to Health Authority and Trust Chairs. This has meant that the centre has formulated policy. Its Regional Offices have vetted local plans and had local Health Authorities monitor their implementation. All of this has assumed an expectation that local management would gladly endorse and enthusiastically follow central policy. The successful delivery of services at the local level has thus been judged by short-term bottom line targets that are determined by political imperatives. A performance management system continues to operate that is designed to identify failings in local trusts so that sanctions can be taken against those that do not succeed. Therefore, superficially, the Government seems to be in control. The strategy for achieving control at the level of the individual hospital has thus been reliant on strong management using industrial and business style techniques. These have sought to increase managerial control over the NHS equivalent of production processes in matters such as bed occupancy, throughput and turnover. To achieve this, there has been a deliberate attempt to reduce the personal discretion which individual clinicians have by exerting budgetary controls on them, and by the introduction of performance indicators and standard setting that makes their performance more transparent. There is a great deal that could be said about the pace of the current management reorganization and its effects on the morale of staff, who suffer constant and debilitating reorganization exhaustion. There is also a view that the concept underlying the present re-organization (in which power will be allegedly devolved to frontline staff, that has been described as ‘earned autonomy’) contains some fundamental errors in its coherence. This has been described as: ‘deeply flawed as it will breed a cadre of immature, conformist managers who instead of focusing on improving population health and care quality will always be looking inwards and upwards to Whitehall’ (p. 5, Calman, Hunter & May 2001). At the local level, NHS Chief Executives seem to be in control. But what is unclear is how this present structural reorganization, which may have cosmetic merit, will alter the real locus of power within the NHS. It is well known that the NHS is a vastly complicated organization, not least because of its size. It employs one million people and is the second biggest employer in the world (after Indian railways). Unlike industrial companies, where the mission, inputs, processes and outputs are clear to all that work in them, the NHS vastly differs. It is comprised of many professional groups, each of whom have particular vested interests that militate against teamwork. All of this means that there is much demarcation between roles. Previous reorganizations have failed to address the distribution of local power and the particular implications of this power for local managerial control. This especially concerns a failure to control the power of the medical profession. Medical power has its origins in the nineteenth century, when medicine was trying to professionalize and distinguish itself from ordinary craftsmen. As a profession it argued that its standards transcend basic honesty and include considerable altruism. As a concession for upholding its own standards, it was given wide autonomy (Harrison & Pollit 1994). This freedom was strengthened at the inception of the NHS, when doctors reluctantly joined the NHS with contractual provisos that left general practitioners as independent contractors and gave consultant medical staff rights to pursue private practice. Direct access to the Chief Medical Officer, and hence the Secretary of State for Health, through the British Medical Association (BMA) and the Royal Colleges was an additional entitlement that still exists. These privileges, reinforced by broader cultural factors in society and within the NHS, confer such things as status, earning power and the right not to be contradicted. The reality is that the medical profession has permeated the decision-making machinery at every level of the NHS. It has therefore a polished history of mediating policies and controlling local decisions to suit its own political ends while remaining unchallenged for having done so. Since 1991 Governments have constantly attempted to empower managers to manage this medical dominance. This intention has been reinforced in the NHS Plan (DOH 2000), in which responsibilities for maintaining surveillance over clinical behaviour and a requirement that the medical profession submit to annual appraisal are just two examples. In theory these recent reforms have put new power into the hands of managers to challenge doctors and to manage and control them by putting them into a line management relationship with NHS Chief executives. Yet in practice, managers choose not to be too intrusive or provide too much resistance to medical opinion that is half reasonable, on the basis that power relationships are stacked against them. The medical profession will quarrel vigorously amongst itself. But if threatened by the laity it becomes fiercely loyal, and will resist encroachment upon its autonomy. Hence, the strategic position of the medical profession is never to be underestimated and it is impossible to analyse the NHS fully without acknowledging the strength of medical dominance within it. Medicine controls a scarce technical expertise, has a monopoly over the knowledge required to prescribe and treat, and has power to define health, illness and health policy. It has influence over all aspects of local NHS organization, most notably through control over its productivity (Flynn 1992). It can be argued that past Governments have not totally ducked the issue of medical dominance and power. Throughout the 1990s, there has been much progress in involving doctors in management through their involvement in clinical directorates. Additionally, doctors' involvement in financial control has done much to modify and modernise their attitudes to management and their own responsibilities to the organization in which they work, after all, it is their clinical decisions that allocate the resources of the NHS. In more recent times, the present Government cited a number of measures aimed at enhancing medical accountability and controlling the efficiency and effectiveness of clinical behaviour. The introduction of Clinical Governance with its emphasis on evidence-based practice and insistence on the use of the findings of the National Institute for Clinical Excellence, the Cochrane Collaboration and the Centre for Dissemination and Reviews looks like a genuine attempt to monitor standards. In its quest to make the medical profession more accountable and transparent, the British Government has given legal powers to NHS managers, who usually are not clinically qualified professionals, to review the results of the audit of practice and to take action accordingly. Not surprisingly, managers lack confidence and legitimacy in dealing with clinical issues. It is also easy for individual doctors to argue that the emphasis on evidence-based practice is an infringement of their clinical freedom. This is difficult to dispute given that caring for the sick is inherently uncertain and that there is an art as well as a science in delivering the care that is needed by the individual patient (Grayson 1997). This stance supports the view that expert clinical decision making relies on experience and professional intuition as well as evidence. Furthermore, doctors could argue that they often have to delay clinically valid treatments because it is they who have responsibility to ration treatments until the NHS can afford to provide them. In a similar move to police medical standards, the Government has set up a Commission for Health Improvement. The Commission's remit is to act as an external inspectorate of the clinical work and performance of hospitals and that of those who deliver primary care to ensure that the best evidence is being used in practice. The results will be made public to expose standards of practice as part of this scrutiny. The Commission's impact has yet to be felt, given that it has spent its first year organizing procedures that will attach blame for any deficiencies of the NHS onto managers. In continuing the long march to make medicine accountable to managers, the Government has tackled the profession head-on in two other significant ways: its professional regulation and its remuneration. The conviction of Dr Harold Shipman for murdering his patients provided unequivocal proof that medical regulation had serious deficiencies. A review of the workings of the General Medical Council has been conducted and has introduced the idea that it should contain lay membership for the first time. New disciplinary mechanisms have been introduced to deal with complaints against doctors. Additionally, the concept of a five-yearly revalidation for doctors is to be introduced. In the wake of reform of its statutory body, clinical governance and organizations like the Commission for Health Improvement, the possibility arises that a profession that was once wholly unregulated will soon protest that it is now part of a blame culture. The Government has also embarked on reviewing the contractual arrangements of doctors to reward and give incentives to those who do most for the NHS. The current contract does not deliver consistently in either the NHS or in the private sector. Hence, the government is keen to manage the existing variations in Consultant performance. This is a highly sensitive area. Medical pay bargaining has sufficient importance to be dealt with by a Cabinet Committee. Any previous attempt to introduce performance-related pay for doctors, which is intended to motivate and increase effectiveness for the individual and the organization, has always been resisted. This system of remuneration presumes that performance can be measured. Doctors have insisted however, that their work is not subject to such measurement. Experience suggests that if the outcome of contractual negotiations is not to the satisfaction of the profession, its response will be to threaten resignation from the NHS and to set up its business in Chambers like the legal profession. At this suggestion the employers will predictably capitulate to the particular demands the doctors are making. The NHS is in a state of constant structural reorganization in its quest to control the service in ways that secure best value for money. Its current reforms are a massive undertaking that is being implemented at a breakneck speed. The structural changes in the new framework are ambitious and their logic is plausible. But like other reorganizations, this is unlikely to deal with the real locus of power in the NHS. Despite some cosmetic evidence to the contrary, there is nothing distinctive within current policies to indicate that the unbridled, historic privilege of the clinical autonomy of doctors will be in any way seriously disturbed. After all, it is the medical profession that is the spending agent of the NHS and it is unlikely that the power and influence that goes with this will be disturbed. As with previous reorganizations, the deckchairs on the foredeck of the Titanic are being are being rearranged yet again!

title: From Secure Agentic AI to Secure Agentic Web: Challenges, Threats, and Future Directions
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agentic systems that plan, memorize, and act in open-world environments. This shift brings new security problems: failures are no longer only unsafe text generation, but can become real harm through tool use, persistent memory, and interaction with untrusted web content. In this survey, we provide a transition-oriented view from Secure Agentic AI to a Secure Agentic Web. We first summarize a component-aligned threat taxonomy covering prompt abuse, environment injection, memory attacks, toolchain abuse, model tampering, and agent network attacks. We then review defense strategies, including prompt hardening, safety-aware decoding, privilege control for tools and APIs, runtime monitoring, continuous red-teaming, and protocol-level security mechanisms. We further discuss how these threats and mitigations escalate in the Agentic Web, where delegation chains, cross-domain interactions, and protocol-mediated ecosystems amplify risks via propagation and composition. Finally, we highlight open challenges for web-scale deployment, such as interoperable identity and authorization, provenance and traceability, ecosystem-level response, and scalable evaluation under adaptive adversaries. Our goal is to connect recent empirical findings with system-level requirements, and to outline practical research directions toward trustworthy agent ecosystems.

title: CCCE: A Continuous Code Calibration Engine for Autonomous Enterprise Codebase Maintenance via Knowledge Graph Traversal and Adaptive Decision Gating
abstract: Enterprise software organizations face an escalating challenge in maintaining the integrity, security, and freshness of codebases that span hundreds of repositories, multiple programming languages, and thousands of interdependent packages. Existing approaches to codebase maintenance -- including static analysis, software composition analysis (SCA), and dependency management tools -- operate in isolation, address only narrow subsets of maintenance concerns, and require substantial manual intervention to propagate changes across interconnected systems. We present the Continuous Code Calibration Engine (CCCE), an event-driven, AI-agentic system that autonomously maintains enterprise codebases throughout the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). The CCCE introduces three key technical innovations: (1) a dynamic knowledge graph with bidirectional traversal algorithms that simultaneously compute forward impact propagation and backward test adequacy analysis; (2) an adaptive multi-stage gating framework that classifies calibration actions into four risk tiers using learned risk-confidence scoring rather than static rules; and (3) a multi-model continuous learning architecture operating at multiple temporal scales to refine calibration strategies, risk models, and organizational policies from operational feedback. We formalize the system's graph model, traversal algorithms, and decision logic, and demonstrate through three representative enterprise scenarios that the CCCE reduces mean time to remediation by enabling coordinated, cross-repository calibrations with human-in-the-loop (HITL) oversight where appropriate. The system generates atomic, semantically verified patches with progressive validation and intelligent rollback capabilities, providing end-to-end traceability from triggering events through calibration execution and outcome learning.

title: ASHP Guidelines on the Safe Use of Automated Dispensing Cabinets
abstract: Address correspondence to Bruce Hawkins ([email protected]). Automated dispensing cabinet (ADC) technology is used to improve patient care, enhance the efficiency and accuracy of medication dispensing in the medication-use system, support medication storage and security, and provide evaluation of ADC-user interactions. ADC use has become widespread in healthcare institutions, with 93% of hospitals using ADCs in their medication-use systems,1 and 70.2% using ADCs as a primary method of maintenance dose distribution.2 Implementation steps and objectives to support an ADC system include the following: Software and hardware technology for optimal operations are available and supported by knowledgeable staff; ADC maintenance is supported with adequate personnel, minimum downtime, and analytical reporting for ordering and restocking; Staff education and competency on ADC operation are supported at a high level. Interfaces to other technologies supporting medication use (eg, intravenous [IV] infusion systems) are created to enable efficient workflows and enhanced medication diversion detection; Interoperability is established with the electronic health record (EHR) and related systems; Safe and secure operation is ensured with real-time reporting functionality of medication diversion; Mechanical operation and inventory management capabilities exist to allow efficient, accurate, and optimized availability of medication; Employment of other technology is used, eg, barcode scanning, biometric identification, special storage and alerting features; and ADCs in procedural and non-acute extended patient care areas (eg, long-term care, ambulatory clinics) have the same standard of medication control as traditional patient care areas. These guidelines address components of ADC technology implementation and important detailed steps to meet and maintain basic ADC requirements. Appropriate, accurate, and timely distribution of medications to patients is a well-established responsibility of pharmacists. Use of ADCs has become the standard of care for the medication-use process in healthcare systems.2 ASHP supports use of ADCs, because they are essential to provide quality patient care, secure storage of medications, and ensure viability of the medication-use process in healthcare organizations. These ASHP guidelines reflect the evolving and increased use of ADCs to improve patient safety and allow secure access to a broad selection of medications. Consideration of the use of ADCs must include serious evaluation of existing and potential opportunities for error and the implementation of mitigating strategies to minimize or prevent such errors. Pharmacists have a professional responsibility to ensure that appropriate policies, procedures, and quality assurance programs are in place to address the safety, accuracy, security, and patient confidentiality of automated pharmacy systems, including ADCs.3 ADCs must provide accurate and controlled storage, dispensing, and monitoring of medications while providing medications in an efficient and safe manner. The ability of ADCs to accomplish these requirements has improved since their introduction in the late 1980s, leading to the technology becoming the primary means of medication distribution.1,2 To be successful at implementing and sustaining ADC benefits, an organization must ensure that the ADC will help optimize the medication-use process and meet financial, operational, and clinical goals of the organization. Technical infrastructure that will best support the system and allow for smooth operation and future growth is of utmost importance. Infrastructure requirements include servers, interfaces, upgrades, integration with other systems, and security. It is essential to ensure that both physical and personnel infrastructure necessary to maintain the system are in place. Servers are typically client-hosted but are becoming increasingly cloud-based as health systems move away from owning and maintaining their own servers.4 Regardless of the hosting approach, servers should be readily available and highly reliable to minimize workflow interruptions. Servers must be adequately sized to store both formulary and user information, as well as transactional information for analytics and reporting, and should be scalable to allow for future growth. Consideration should also be given to minimizing the amount of redundant software maintenance (eg, formulary maintenance). Depending on an organization’s size, an ADC server might be a single standalone server. Larger organizations and integrated delivery networks (IDNs) may employ integrated servers that work together but physically separate different data components into separate servers. Options for server redundancy to offer protection and limit interruptions in the event of unplanned downtime must also be considered. A range of options are available, from data refreshes every few hours to more frequent data refreshes that support minimal losses in the event of unplanned downtime. Partnering with the information technology (IT) department is essential for proper server maintenance, such as operating system patches and security software to protect against viruses and malware, as well as the integrity of frequent data backups. Maintenance may be supplied internally by the system for virtual machines or by the vendor (more commonly for standalone servers). In either case, IT should be engaged to assist and help coordinate proper server security. Finally, an organizational downtime and recovery policy and procedure should be developed and implemented to minimize disruptions in patient care. With the growth of large healthcare IDNs and proliferation of multiple electronic clinical applications used within healthcare systems, ADC vendors have moved toward integrated platforms that simplify and standardize system maintenance. The ADC system must work seamlessly with other clinical systems, which include at a minimum EHRs, pharmacy information systems (PISs), and admission/discharge/transfer systems. Each of these other systems serve as the source of primary data for the formulary, barcodes, patient information, medication profile, and medication orders. The ADC provides source information for other clinical systems through interfaces based on Health Level Seven International (HL7) standards. Affected clinical systems include inventory information for the PIS, dispense information for billing systems (for organizations that charge on dispense), usage information for inventory management systems, and user information for a domain management system. Finally, many systems also use interface engines to streamline system connectivity, especially when multiple systems come from the same vendor. During the build phase of ADC system implementation, all interfaces must be thoroughly tested to ensure that both accurate and current information is transmitted into the ADC system.
